title: Twelve-Tone Technique
intro: Schoenberg's twelve-tone method orders all twelve pitch classes into a row and builds a piece from that row and its transformations, so that no pitch class is emphasised as a tonic.

blocks.text: A twelve-tone row (series) is an ordering of the twelve pitch classes, each used once. The four basic forms:

items: Prime (P): the row as written. P0 is the row transposed to start on 0; Pn starts on n.
Inversion (I): every interval turned upside down. In starts on n.
Retrograde (R): the prime backwards. Rn is the retrograde of Pn.

blocks.text: With twelve transpositions of each, a row has 48 forms (fewer for symmetric rows). Composers choose row forms and distribute the notes among voices, chords and registers freely: the row fixes the order of pitch classes, not their octave, rhythm or texture.

A 12 × 12 matrix lists all forms. Write P0 across the top and I0 down the left (the inversion: each entry of P0 subtracted from 12). Each row of the matrix is a P form read left to right (R read right to left); each column is an I form read top to bottom (RI bottom to top). Row n is P(I0's nth entry).

blocks.source:
def matrix(p0):
    """Rows are P forms, columns I forms. p0: list of 12 pitch classes starting on 0."""
    i0 = [(-x) % 12 for x in p0]
    return [[(x + start) % 12 for x in p0] for start in i0]

# The row of Berg's Violin Concerto (1935), transposed to start on 0:
p0 = [0, 3, 7, 11, 2, 5, 9, 1, 4, 6, 8, 10]
for r in matrix(p0):
    print(" ".join("0123456789TE"[x] for x in r))

blocks.text: Berg's row is famous because its first nine notes form a chain of alternating major and minor triads (G minor, D major, A minor, E major: G B♭ D F♯ A C E G♯ B) and its last four (B C♯ E♭ F) are a whole-tone segment that opens the Bach chorale 'Es ist genug', which the concerto quotes. Twelve-tone writing need not sound like random atonality.

blocks.text: After 1945 composers such as Boulez, Stockhausen and Babbitt extended the idea of ordering to durations, dynamics and articulation (total serialism). Babbitt also explored combinatoriality: rows whose first half (hexachord) can combine with the first half of a transformed form to make all twelve pitch classes, which lets two row forms sound together without doubling a note.

Sources: Straus, J. N. (2016). Introduction to Post-Tonal Theory, 4th ed. W. W. Norton; Perle, G. (1991). Serial Composition and Atonality, 6th ed. University of California Press; Babbitt, M. (1960). Twelve-tone invariants as compositional determinants. Musical Quarterly 46(2); Pople, A. (1991). Berg: Violin Concerto. Cambridge University Press.
